newsitem.title: USA: US CRUDE OUTLOOK - Rangebound prices wait for jolt.
newsitem.headline: US CRUDE OUTLOOK - Rangebound prices wait for jolt.

text.p: U.S. crudes have failed to move out of established price ranges in recent weeks, giving the market a static feel heading into the first week of December trading, traders said Monday.
Outright crude values have been stuck between around $23.20-$24.95 a barrel for West Texas Intermediate/Cushing since the "wide" range trading day on NYMEX November 20.
Outright crudes were not seen making a dramatic move out of that constraint this week.
Last week's news that Iraq agreed to the terms of the long-delayed U.N. oil-for-food accord was met with a milder-than-expected sell-off in spot crude, leaving some players scratching their heads.
"You would think the market would move more with the potential for Iraqi oil and OPEC rolling over their quota," said Tom Bentz, energy analyst for ING Derivatives.
OPEC ended their meeting last week by extending their quota limits on crude output at 25.03 million barrels per day.

Market weariness to Iraqi developments was likely due to sentiment fourth quarter demand would absorb the extra barrels, and an attitude of "I'll see it when I believe it" to any news concerning Saddam Hussein's Iraq.
"Demand in the fourth quarter is running at a high rate, but I would be worried about the first quarter (for the Iraqi return to the market)," said Bentz.
Cash crude traders said the short December trading month should provoke refiner interest in the market this week after the post-Thanksgiving Day holiday lull disappears.
Domestic grade differentials were expected to fluctuate within established patterns: the sweet grades staying firm and the sour barrels pressured.
"I think the LLS (Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James) will be up on the continued arb," said a Texas trader.
LLS starts the week at a 90 cents premium to the Jan WTI/Cushing, but may see some pressure to the low 60's before moving back to firmer levels approaching a $1.00 premium, the trader said.
Perceptions in the market point to uneconomical arbitrage opportunities for bringing Brent crude to the U.S. Current screen numbers put the January WTI/Brent spread at around $1.00.

Sour grades have been treading in weak territory for some time, hit by fundamental oversupply as Canadian barrels and U.S. government sales of Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) stocks deflated market values.
Additional pressure will be applied on the sours once the first Iraqi crude exports appear.
"When Iraqi crude comes out, it will get ugly for the sour grades since the Urals will get killed, and be displaced to the U.S.," reasoned one cash trader.

West Texas Sour/Midland was presently talked at a differential from $1.70-$1.80 below the Jan WTI/Cushing. The trader said that mark could slip to a $2.00-$2.50 discount when Baghdad starts pumping again.
Cash traders said Iraqi oil will likely appear in late December or early January.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali must still report to the Security Council that the oil deal is ready. The sanctions committee on Iraq scheduled a Tuesday meeting, and will be briefed by the secretariat on where the deal stands.
Inspectors from Dutch-firm Saybolt were expected in join Lloyds Register personnel in trekking to Iraq this week in order to finalize inspection of key monitoring facilities.
--New York Energy Desk, +1 212 859 1828
